title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class) and a shared-initial-candidate paired design, we produced one generator output per task with gpt-5-mini and evaluated that same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could invoke ≤1 repair iteration. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false for every guarded episode. We (1) present a concise, literature-grounded positioning and nearest-work comparison; (2) provide a compact formal definition of the binary outcome and a concrete scoring example drawn from archived artifacts; (3) explain why the shared-generation paired design produced a ceiling result and propose concrete, artifact-grounded design changes for future confirmatory studies.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs promise to convert operator intent into actionable network configuration commands, but syntactically plausible outputs can violate stateful workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing hazardous uplink switchover). Prior work therefore advocates integrating verification, emulation, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Our preregistered confirmatory question (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) asked: Does integrating an executable emulator validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair marginal effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: a single generator output per task was scored under both baseline (LLM-only) and guarded (validator±repair) conditions. This design maximizes internal validity for measuring validator impact on identical candidates but, as preregistered, reduces the probability that the repair subsystem will be exercised when the generator routinely produces valid candidates. We report the preregistered confirmatory statistics and use archived execution artifacts to explain the degenerate (ceiling) outcome and to give concrete methodological recommendations for follow-up confirmatory runs.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation-grounded benchmarks and NetOps verification tools demonstrate that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: closed-loop emulation exposes sequencing and stateful errors (make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, ordered operations). Complementary work proposes tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translate-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair). However, few published experiments isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator on identical generator outputs; most prior evaluations conflate generator variance with verifier efficacy.

Nearest-work comparison (compact):
- Protogeros et al. (arXiv:2604.22513): benchmark for LLM-driven config repair; focuses on generator/repair performance across model outputs (independent-generation emphasis). Differs: independent-generation design; less focus on a paired, shared-candidate marginal test. 
- NetConfArena (arXiv:2608.23179): executable closed-loop benchmark; demonstrates failures visible only under emulation. Differs: broad benchmark; not designed as a paired marginal isolation of validator effects on identical outputs. 
- MeshAgent (DOI:10.1145/3771567): prototype system for reliable management with LLMs; proposes guardrails and tool integration. Differs: system design focus, multi-stage agent pipelines; not a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment. 
- Lightyear / BGP verification (DOI:10.1145/3603269.3604842): formal verification emphasis for control-plane correctness. Differs: verification formalisms for routing; distinct problem scope. 
- Position/architecture reports (arXiv:2607.22947, arXiv:2604.18233): propose translation and digital-twin validations as safety measures. Our study complements these by providing a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design that holds the generator fixed to measure validator/repair marginal effects.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) before execution. The confirmatory estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, tested with exact two-sided McNemar; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Planned: N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine; 40 tasks each). Preregistration hash: 0bfc96e9afceed579f04a06dcbad2387ee4acca970559d9a4faa165893f4fe50.

Task generation and shared-generation design. Tasks were generated deterministically (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). For each task a single shared initial candidate was produced by the declared model (gpt-5-mini). Execution accounting: planned_episode_count=240; completed_episode_count=240; model_calls_used=120 (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=120); declared_model_version=gpt-5-mini; model_calls_used recorded in execution manifest.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). The validator executes the candidate in an emulated state checker and emits a structured validator_trace that includes validation_before/after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy permitted at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and provider traces were archived when generated.

Formal binary outcome (confirmatory label). The pass/fail label used in the McNemar test was derived deterministically from the validator/scorer outputs as follows (archived scoring pipeline identifiers and versions are shown in the execution artifacts):
- Scoring engine: scorer_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, scorer_version = 5.0, scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation".
- Decision logic (applied after emulation): PASS if validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0 AND scorer returns score == 1 (score_reason_code == "VALID_CONFIGURATION"); otherwise FAIL. Repair application does not change the original shared candidate label in the baseline condition; in the guarded condition a repair may be attempted if violation_count>0, and the guarded outcome reflects validation_after on the post-repair configuration.

Concrete scoring example (archived artifact). For pair_id = pair-000001 (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json): normalized_response =
"interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.violation_count = 0; score = 1; score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION". Under the decision logic above this episode is labeled PASS. The guarded episode for the same pair records the same normalized_response and validator fields, and is also labeled PASS; repair_applied = false in the guarded trace.

Instrumentation and contamination controls. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets (container image checksums + deterministic seeds) between tasks, duplicate-output detection, and provider-call audits. Contamination/tracking artifacts and deterministic_reconciliation were recorded; no exclusions or contamination flags occurred.

sections.discussion:
Why the ceiling occurred. The paired shared-generation design was chosen to isolate the validator/repair marginal effect on identical generator outputs. In the archived task bank and with the frozen prompt/model configuration the generator produced valid candidates for every task; therefore the guarded validator had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. Statistically this produces zero discordant pairs (n_10 = n_01 = 0), yielding McNemar p = 1.0 and a degenerate bootstrap CI. This degenerate outcome is a direct, artifact-grounded consequence of the observed concordant data and the preregistered resampling scheme (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10000).

Design trade-offs and concrete follow-ups. The shared-generation paired design increases internal validity but risks under-exercising repair when the generator is well-calibrated. Using fields already present in task manifests (difficulty.level; dependency_rule_count; required_command_count) the archived artifacts permit targeted follow-ups that increase generator error incidence without inventing new data. Based on these artifacts we recommend, for future confirmatory runs seeking to measure repair utility: (1) relax shared-generation and allow independent generation per condition or block-structured pairing so the guard can intercept generator-induced faults; (2) prespecify targeted selection of tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with high dependency_rule_count from the manifest to raise invalid-candidate probability; (3) include prompt-perturbation arms (the preregistration contained exploratory perturbation plans) to induce controlled generator variability; (4) expand repair budget in exploratory arms to study repair convergence behavior and repair-call costs. These recommendations are evidence-driven and do not alter archived run artifacts.

Operational implications. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (validation_before/after, touched fields, violation codes) supports operator auditability, reproducible after-action review, and third-party inspection. The archived execution artifacts provide complete provider-call audits and validator traces which, in production-like deployments, would be useful for operator trust and forensic review.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: high—deterministic provisioning, provider-call audits, and zero exclusions. Construct validity: limited by the validator's encoded workflow policies that derive from synthetic task payloads; the emulator does not capture every vendor-specific behavior or partial observability condition. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline ≈0.40; target absolute reduction = 0.15) were violated by observed baseline = 0.00, rendering the confirmatory test uninformative about the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) to measure the marginal effect of an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline on identical LLM-generated candidates. All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing identical perfect success rates for baseline and guarded conditions (n_11=120; McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate a preregistered paired protocol that cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and we provide artifact-grounded diagnostics and concrete design recommendations (relax shared-generation, target 'very_hard' tasks, add perturbation arms, expand repair budget) to ensure repair utility is observable in future confirmatory trials. All primary execution and analysis artifacts are archived and checksummed in the evidence bundle to enable reproducible follow-up studies.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
